clinicalPearls: Classic presentation is sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain of rapid onset, often with nausea and vomiting, most commonly in adolescents and young men but also seen in neonates
Examination typically shows a swollen, exquisitely tender, high-riding testis that may lie transversely (horizontal lie) with an absent cremasteric reflex
It is a time-critical surgical emergency: testicular salvage is high if detorsion occurs within about six hours and falls sharply thereafter
The bell-clapper anomaly, in which the tunica vaginalis invests the testis abnormally, predisposes to intravaginal torsion and is often bilateral
Diagnosis is fundamentally clinical; imaging should never delay surgery when torsion is strongly suspected
Colour Doppler ultrasound showing absent or reduced intratesticular blood flow supports the diagnosis, but a normal study does not reliably exclude it

Definitive treatment is emergency scrotal exploration with detorsion and orchidopexy of the affected testis, plus fixation of the contralateral testis because the predisposing anomaly is usually bilateral
Manual detorsion may be attempted as a temporising measure but does not replace surgical exploration and fixation
reference.pathophysiology: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that obstructs venous drainage first and then arterial inflow, producing ischaemia and, if unrelieved, haemorrhagic infarction of the testis. The intravaginal form, most common in adolescents, is facilitated by the bell-clapper deformity where the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis and epididymis completely, allowing the testis to rotate freely within it. Extravaginal torsion occurs in neonates when the entire tunica and its contents twist above the level of attachment. The degree of twisting and the duration of ischaemia determine the likelihood of viability.
additionalDifferentials: Torsion of a testicular or epididymal appendage (appendix testis)
additionalInvestigations: Urgent surgical exploration when clinical suspicion is high (imaging must not delay this)
Colour Doppler ultrasound to assess intratesticular blood flow when the diagnosis is uncertain and readily available
Urinalysis, which is typically normal and helps distinguish from infection
Assessment of the contralateral testis given the frequently bilateral anatomical predisposition
redFlags: Testicular torsion is a urological emergency; salvage depends on detorsion within roughly six hours, so exploration must not be delayed for investigations
Sudden severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex until proven otherwise
Neonatal torsion, which may present with a firm, discoloured, painless scrotal swelling
Progressive testicular ischaemia leading to non-viable testis and need for orchidectomy
reference.prognosis: Testicular viability depends critically on time to detorsion, with excellent salvage within a few hours and progressively poorer outcomes beyond six to twelve hours; a non-viable testis requires orchidectomy, and infarction may later affect fertility.
pitfalls: Attributing acute scrotal pain to epididymo-orchitis and delaying surgical exploration
Waiting for or relying on ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high
Assuming a normal Doppler study excludes torsion, especially in intermittent or partial torsion
Failing to fix the contralateral testis, leaving it at risk of subsequent torsion
Dismissing intermittent testicular pain that may represent recurrent torsion-detorsion
management: Undertake immediate surgical scrotal exploration and detorsion as a time-critical emergency, since salvage falls sharply with delay and imaging must not hold up surgery
Fix a viable testis with orchidopexy, or perform orchidectomy if the testis is non-viable at exploration
Fix the contralateral testis at the same operation, as the predisposing bell-clapper anomaly is frequently bilateral
Attempt manual detorsion with analgesia as a temporising measure only if definitive surgery will be delayed
Use colour Doppler ultrasound only when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and immediately available, never delaying exploration
Counsel on possible effects on fertility and, after orchidectomy, on cosmesis and prosthesis, with appropriate follow-up
Refer urgently to urology or surgery on clinical suspicion
